Case: Stiff-person syndrome is a rare neurological disorder characterized by rigidity and painful spasms of the trunk and
limbs, and patients sometimes have difficulty in walking due to rigid toe deformities. This is a case report of a 76-year-old
woman suffering from stiff-person syndrome with painful rigid toe deformities regained walking ability after metatarsal
osteotomy and cutting of the toe extensors for all toes in the left foot.

Case Report
76-year-old woman visited our department of orthopaedic
surgery complaining of difficulty in walking due to painful
toe deformities in the left foot. The symptoms in her left limb
started at 61 years of age, when she felt a spasm in her leg. At 63
years of age, she consulted a neurologist in our university hospital.
She tested positive for anti-GAD antibodies, and a drug challenge
test with diazepam alleviated the muscle spasm in her leg. Based
on these findings combined with other symptoms and episodes
meeting the relevant criteria, she was diagnosed as having stiffperson syndrome. The spasticity and rigidity of her limb were
controlled by administration of diazepam and corticosteroid.

A

At 6 years after the diagnosis (69 years of age), claw toe
deformities appeared on all of her left toes. The deformities
became more rigid and painful with passing years, and she finally
visited our orthopaedic department complaining of difficulty in
walking. At that time, rigid claw toe deformities existed on all toes
in her left foot with painful callosities on the dorsum of the
interphalangeal joints and the plantar side of the metatarsophalangeal joint of the hallux (Figs. 1 and 2). The impairment of
walking ability was mainly caused by the protrusion of the first
metatarsal head and the painful callosities on its plantar side.
Conservative treatment, including insoles and pads, was
not satisfactory, so we decided to perform surgery. Metatarsal
bone shortening osteotomies were planned because the dislocation of every metatarsophalangeal joint had been persisted
for at least a year and it was irreducible on preoperative examination. The surgery was performed under spinal anesthesia. We used 3 longitudinal incisions: 1 on the medial side of the
first ray and 2 on the dorsal side between the second and third
metatarsals and fourth and fifth metatarsals. We shortened the
first metatarsal bone by 4 mm with a Z-shaped osteotomy. For
the lesser toes, Weil osteotomies were performed to shorten the
second to fifth metatarsal bones by 4 mm (Fig. 3). The amount
of shortening of the first metatarsal bone was preoperatively
estimated by the overlapping of the first proximal phalanx and
the first metatarsal head on the anteroposterior plain radiograph (Fig. 2). The same amount of shortening was planned for

extensors to avoid recurrence of the toe deformities. Finally,
longitudinal K-wire fixations were performed (Fig. 4).
Postoperatively, the patient was allowed to bear weight
on the heel as tolerated using a heel weight-bearing shoe until
6 weeks. The K-wires were removed at 4 weeks after the surgery. After the removal of K-wires, active and passive range-ofmotion exercise of the metatarsophalangeal joint was utilized.
Controlling her blood sugar level was difficult because
she had a steroid-induced diabetes mellitus, but no wound
complication or pin-site infection occurred.
At the latest follow-up in our clinic (18 months postoperatively), she was able to walk without pain in her foot,
although the recurrence of the deformity was observed in the
fifth toe (Figs. 5 and 6). She did not have any episodes of spasm
in her trunk, but she had a chronic back pain with mild lumbar
spine deformity. No pain medication other than antispasmodic
drugs was needed for her back pain.

The clinical manifestations in the present case were restricted
to the left limb and thus classified as SLS.
The mainstay of therapy for stiff-person syndrome is
pharmacologic treatment. The first-line drug for stiff-person
syndrome is diazepam, a GABA-enhancing drug, which can
alleviate painful spasms and rigidity11. In fact, response to
diazepam is included in the diagnostic criteria for stiffperson syndrome. Other drugs such as antiepileptic drugs,
antispastic drugs, and immunomodulatory drugs are also
used in the treatment of stiff-person syndrome8-10, 13, 14. The
duration of stiff-person syndrome can vary from several
weeks to more than 10 years3, 4, 8. After a period of stiff-person
syndrome, the limb deformities and spinal lordosis become
rigid regardless of drug control.
Despite several reports on medical therapy to control spasticity in stiff-person syndrome8, 10, 11, no reports have described
management of rigid deformities. About one-half of patients with
stiff-person syndrome become wheelchair-bound3. Up to 65% of
patients cannot perform daily activities independently8. In the
present case, painful foot deformities restricted her activities of
daily living. Under adequate drug control of the spasms, surgical
correction was an effective intervention for the rigid foot deformities to regain walking ability and maintain this ability for at least
18 months. This is the first report of surgical intervention for toe
deformities in a patient with stiff-person syndrome.
The resection arthroplasty, in which all of the metatarsal
head was removed, could be an alternative surgical procedure.
The reason we did not perform the resection arthroplasty was

that this procedure disables active toe movements, which increase
the risk of falling for the patient with muscle spasms.
In summary, a patient with stiff-person syndrome regained her walking ability by metatarsal shortening osteotomy
and cutting of the toe extensors for her painful toe deformities.
Surgical intervention is a powerful treatment option when a
patient has developed rigid and painful toe deformities despite
adequate pharmacological treatment. n
